options: Amps (A), from the label or a clamp meter
fields.hint: Pick Amps if the appliance only shows amps or you measured the current; the watts are then worked out from volts × amps × power factor.

fields.name: watts
fields.label: Appliance power
fields.hint: From the rating label. Used in Watts mode. 1,000 W for one hour is exactly one unit.

fields.name: amps
fields.label: Current
fields.hint: Used in Amps mode only. From the label or a clamp meter reading.

fields.name: hours
fields.label: Hours a day
fields.hint: How long it runs each day. For a fridge or AC use the hours the compressor actually runs.

fields.name: days
fields.label: Days
fields.hint: Enter 1 for units a day, 30 for a month.

fields.label: Supply type (Amps mode)

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage (Amps mode)
fields.hint: 230 V in Pakistan, 120 V in the US, 400 V line-to-line for three phase, 12 or 24 V for a battery.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor (Amps mode, AC only)
fields.hint: Motors and fans about 0.8, heaters and irons 1.0. Ignored for DC.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Tariff
fields.hint: Your per-unit rate from the bill; the pre-filled rate is the unprotected slab for three to four hundred units.

answer: One electricity unit is one kilowatt hour (kWh): a {{out.watts|int}} W appliance running for one hour uses exactly one unit, so {{out.hours|int}} hour a day for {{out.days|int}} days is {{out.units|2}} units. Units = watts × hours ÷ 1,000, or from amps: volts × amps × power factor × hours ÷ 1,000. Enter your appliance's watts or amps and hours to get its units.
how: {{out.watts|int}} W × {{out.hours|2}} h a day × {{out.days|int}} days ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|2}} units (kWh). In Amps mode the watts come first from volts × amps × power factor (× the square root of three for three phase), then the same step.
key_facts: One electricity unit = one kilowatt hour (kWh) = 1,000 watts used for one hour; a {{out.watts|int}} W appliance uses one unit every hour it runs, and a hundred-watt bulb takes ten hours to use one unit.
Units = watts × hours ÷ 1,000: an {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W fan for {{ex.0.out.hours|int}} hours a day uses {{ex.0.out.units|2}} units in {{ex.0.out.days|int}} days.

Units from amps = volts × amps × power factor × hours ÷ 1,000: an appliance drawing {{ex.1.out.amps|int}} A at {{ex.1.out.volts|int}} V with a {{ex.1.out.pf|1}} power factor is {{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W and uses {{ex.1.out.units|1}} units in {{ex.1.out.days|int}} days at {{ex.1.out.hours|int}} hours a day.
On DC the power factor is one: {{ex.2.out.amps|int}} A from a {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V battery is {{ex.2.out.watts|int}} W, which is {{ex.2.out.units|2}} units over {{ex.2.out.hours|int}} hours.

formula.text: units (kWh) = W × h × days ÷ 1000; W = V × A × PF (DC: PF = 1; three phase: × √3)
lines: W = power in watts, h = hours a day, days = number of days
V = supply voltage, A = current in amps, PF = power factor
From amp hours: units = Ah × V ÷ 1000

p: Exactly one. The unit on a Pakistani electricity bill, and on most bills worldwide, is the kilowatt hour: one thousand watts used for one hour. A {{out.watts|int}} W appliance running for one hour, an {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W fan running for about twelve and a half hours, and a ten-watt LED bulb running for a hundred hours all use one unit. The meter counts these units and the bill multiplies them by the rate of your slab.

So 1 unit in watts is not a fixed number of watts; it is watts times hours. Watts say how fast an appliance uses electricity, units say how much it has used. That is why a {{ex.3.out.watts|int}} W AC for {{ex.3.out.hours|int}} hours a day ({{ex.3.out.units|int}} units a month) costs far more than a {{out.watts|int}} W iron for one hour a day, even though the watts are the same.

sections.h2: How to calculate electricity units from watts
p: Take the watts from the appliance label, multiply by the hours it runs in a day, and divide by one thousand. That is the units a day; multiply by the days in the month for the monthly figure. An {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W ceiling fan for {{ex.0.out.hours|int}} hours a day is {{ex.0.out.units|2}} units over {{ex.0.out.days|int}} days.

Use the real running hours, not the hours the appliance is switched on. A fridge compressor runs about a third of the time, and an inverter AC draws far less than its rated watts for most of the hour; the appliance load calculator and the AC units calculator use planning averages for those.

sections.h2: Amps to kWh: units from a current reading
p: Some labels give amps instead of watts, and a clamp meter always reads amps. Switch to Amps mode: the calculator first converts to watts with volts × amps × power factor, then applies the same hours and days. At {{ex.1.out.volts|int}} V and a {{ex.1.out.pf|1}} power factor, {{ex.1.out.amps|int}} A is {{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W, which over {{ex.1.out.hours|int}} hours a day comes to {{ex.1.out.units|1}} units in {{ex.1.out.days|int}} days.

Set the power factor to one for a heater, iron or geyser and about {{d.pf_mixed|1}} for a motor, fan or compressor. For a three-phase motor the volts are the line-to-line {{d.v_3ph|int}} V and the calculator multiplies by the square root of three.

sections.h2: Amp hours to units: battery energy in kWh
p: A battery is labelled in amp hours. Multiply the Ah by the battery volts and divide by one thousand to get the kWh it stores: a {{ex.4.out.ah|int}} Ah, {{ex.4.out.volts|int}} V battery holds {{ex.4.out.units|1}} units. Only part of that is usable: about half for a tubular battery, so the battery capacity calculator sizes a bank from the appliance watts, not from the raw kWh.

The same rule covers a DC load in Amps mode with the supply set to DC: {{ex.2.out.amps|int}} A from a {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V battery is {{ex.2.out.watts|int}} W, or {{ex.2.out.units|2}} units over {{ex.2.out.hours|int}} hours, with no power factor.

examples.title: Ceiling fan: {{out.watts|int}} W for {{out.hours|int}} hours a day
examples.text: {{out.watts|int}} W × {{out.hours|int}} h × {{out.days|int}} days ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|2}} units a month. One fan running most of the day is about one unit a day.

examples.title: Amps mode: a {{out.amps|int}} A appliance at {{out.volts|int}} V
examples.text: {{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.amps|int}} A × {{out.pf|1}} power factor = {{out.watts|int}} W. {{out.watts|int}} W × {{out.hours|int}} h × {{out.days|int}} days ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|1}} units a month.

examples.title: DC load: {{out.amps|int}} A from a {{out.volts|int}} V battery
examples.text: DC has no power factor, so {{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.amps|int}} A = {{out.watts|int}} W. Over {{out.hours|int}} hours that is {{out.units|2}} units, which is what the battery must supply.

examples.title: Inverter AC at its {{out.watts|int}} W average for {{out.hours|int}} hours a day
examples.text: {{out.watts|int}} W × {{out.hours|int}} h × {{out.days|int}} days ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|int}} units a month at an average draw of about one kilowatt. Rated watts would overstate this; the AC units calculator explains the average.

examples.title: Amp hours: a {{out.ah|int}} Ah, {{out.volts|int}} V battery
examples.text: {{out.ah|int}} Ah × {{out.volts|int}} V ÷ 1,000 = {{out.units|1}} units of stored energy. About half is usable on a tubular battery and about {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} on lithium.

mistakes: Mixing up watts and units. Watts are a rate; units are watts × hours ÷ 1,000. A {{out.watts|int}} W appliance does not use {{out.watts|int}} units.
Using the hours an appliance is switched on instead of the hours it draws power. A fridge or AC compressor cycles; count the running hours.
Forgetting the power factor in Amps mode. Volts × amps gives VA; a motor's watts are about {{d.pf_mixed|1}} of that. For DC there is no power factor.

Reading the AC's rated watts as its average. A 1.5 ton inverter AC is rated at about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.running_w|int}} W but averages about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.avg_w|int}} W over an hour.
safety: A clamp meter is clipped round one live conductor only, never round the whole cable; if you are not sure, ask a licensed electrician to take the reading.

faq.a: One. A unit on the bill is a kilowatt hour: {{out.watts|int}} W used for one hour. A thousand-watt heater uses one unit an hour; a hundred-watt load takes ten hours to use one unit.

There is no fixed answer because a unit is watts × hours. One unit is {{out.watts|int}} W for one hour, {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W for about twelve and a half hours, or a ten-watt bulb for a hundred hours.

faq.q: How do I calculate electricity units per day?
faq.a: Watts × hours a day ÷ 1,000. An {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} W fan for {{ex.0.out.hours|int}} hours is {{ex.0.out.watts|int}} × {{ex.0.out.hours|int}} ÷ 1,000, under one unit a day and {{ex.0.out.units|2}} units a month.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to kWh?
faq.a: Multiply amps by volts and power factor to get watts, then by hours and divide by 1,000. {{ex.1.out.amps|int}} A at {{ex.1.out.volts|int}} V and {{ex.1.out.pf|1}} power factor is {{ex.1.out.watts|int}} W, or {{ex.1.out.units|1}} units over {{ex.1.out.days|int}} days at {{ex.1.out.hours|int}} hours a day.

faq.q: How many units does a 1.5 ton AC use per hour?
faq.a: About one unit an hour for an inverter AC at its average draw of about {{a.ac-split-1-5ton-inverter.avg_w|int}} W, and more in a hot room or at full speed. The AC units calculator gives the figure for each AC type and set point.

faq.q: How many units does a 200 Ah battery hold?
faq.a: {{ex.4.out.ah|int}} Ah × {{ex.4.out.volts|int}} V ÷ 1,000 = {{ex.4.out.units|1}} units. Only about half of that is usable on a tubular battery, and the UPS loses some more as heat; the battery backup time calculator gives the real hours.

faq.q: Does using more units raise my sanctioned load?
faq.a: No. Units are energy over the month; the sanctioned load is the kW your connection may draw at any moment. The sanctioned load calculator works that out from your appliances.

faq.q: How much does one unit cost?
faq.a: It depends on your slab and DISCO. Take the units from this page to the electricity bill calculator, which applies the current tariff, fixed charges and taxes.
